charvel_dk24_hh.pickups: Bridge: direct-mount Custom Seymour Duncan Full Shred TB-10 (Trembucker; Alnico V bar, ~14.6 k ohm DC, resonant peak ~5.5 kHz, Duncan EQ chart bass 4 / mid 4 / treble 8). Neck: direct-mount Seymour Duncan Alnico II Pro APH-1N (Alnico II bar, ~7.6 k ohm DC, resonant peak ~7.1 kHz, bass 7 / mid 4 / treble 8). Pickup models are from Charvel's spec sheet; the electrical figures are from retailer listings of the standard catalogue pickups (Charvel calls the bridge unit 'Custom', so it may differ slightly).

positions.sound: Hot, tight, bright with slightly scooped mids (Full Shred): fast attack, clear low strings. Series = full output; parallel = thinner, brighter, lower output, still hum-cancelling.
positions.suits: High-gain rhythm, palm mutes, pinch harmonics, crunch, cutting leads. Because the pickup is bright and mid-light, leads often want amp mids up and presence down; parallel suits twang and bright cleans.

positions.selects: Both outer coils (one coil from each pickup)
positions.sound: Widest coil spacing: airy, hollow, Tele-middle / Strat-like in parallel; a fat, wide pseudo-humbucker in series.
positions.suits: Clean arpeggios, funk, 80s cleans, snappy modern clean leads. Parallel has low output, so raise amp level or add a compressor; expect less low end, so less bass cut is needed.

positions.sound: Full but open; scooped mids with both the neck's roundness and the bridge's edge.
positions.suits: Clean chords, edge-of-breakup rhythm, jangly parts. Under high gain it can get congested; lower gain or bass.

positions.selects: Both inside coils (one coil from each pickup)
positions.sound: Closer coil spacing than position 2: a little rounder and quackier in parallel, the classic in-between notch tone.
positions.suits: Funk strumming, quack, glassy cleans, Plini-style split-coil lines with compression.

positions.sound: Warm, sweet and soft-attacked (Alnico II), moderate output; full lows, smooth top. Parallel = clearer and more single-coil-like.
positions.suits: Singing/creamy leads above the 12th fret, jazz cleans (tone rolled), legato. Under gain cut bass before the amp or it gets woofy; add presence if it turns dull.

charvel_dk24_hh.toggle: Two-way mini-toggle: down = all series, up = all parallel (Charvel spec sheet). It changes how the selected coils are joined: in positions 1 and 5 the humbucker's own two coils run in series (normal humbucker) or parallel; in positions 2 and 4 the two selected single coils (one from each pickup) run in series or parallel, as traced by an owner. Series = louder, thicker, more low mids, darker resonant peak; parallel = lower output, brighter and clearer, more headroom. All settings pair two coils, so they should remain hum-cancelling. What the toggle does in position 3 is not documented in the sources found.
charvel_dk24_hh.tone_control: No-load tone pot: behaves as a normal tone control from 1 to 9, and at 10 (it clicks into a detent) the tone circuit is removed from the signal entirely, giving a slightly stronger, brighter, more defined signal than a conventional pot at maximum. Rolling just off 10 is a quick way to take a little edge off; 3-6 is the jazz/creamy-lead zone.
charvel_dk24_hh.notes: One volume and one tone control with the 5-way blade and mini-toggle. Charvel's page for this exact model returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher, so the switching text is taken from Charvel spec text quoted in search results; body/neck woods, scale length (Charvel Dinky standard is 25.5 in), fretboard radius and bridge model were NOT re-verified in this session and are left out. An older-model review mentions the Full Shred SH-10B at the bridge on earlier versions. An owner thread warns that factory wiring can vary/be miswired, so verify positions by ear (tap the coils).

les_paul.differences: Shorter scale (24.75 in vs 25.5 in): lower string tension, easier bends, slightly warmer and less snappy, low strings less tight. Two full humbuckers with no in-between single-coil sounds: thicker low mids, more sustain and compression, smoother top. Compared with the DK24's bright, mid-light Full Shred bridge and airy split positions, a Les Paul generally puts more 200-500 Hz and less top into the same preset, and its neck pickup is much fuller in the bass. Output depends on the actual pickups: vintage-style (PAF-type) Les Paul pickups are lower output than the 14.6 k Full Shred, hotter modern ones are similar, so gain compensation can go either way.

compensations.action: Re-check input level/gain first: play the hardest chord and match how hard the amp is being driven (trim the input or the amp gain a notch)
compensations.why: Pickup output difference changes gain, compression and noise before any EQ difference matters.

compensations.action: Raise the pre-amp low cut or boost level slightly, or lower amp Bass 1-2 notches
compensations.why: More low-mid content and a looser low string need more tightening before the distortion.

compensations.action: Cut 2-3 dB around 200-400 Hz after the amp if chords are thick
compensations.why: Les Paul low-mid build-up is the usual cause of mud in a preset made on a superstrat.

compensations.action: Add Presence/Treble 1 notch or move the mic slightly toward the cap
compensations.why: Less top end and bite than the Full Shred bridge and the no-load tone circuit.

compensations.action: For cleans made on positions 2/4, use the Les Paul's middle position, lower the guitar volume to 6-8 and reduce amp bass; add compression and a little 3-5 kHz
compensations.why: There is no split-coil quack; the middle position with reduced volume is the nearest substitute.

compensations.action: On the neck pickup under gain, cut more bass before the amp and consider lowering the pickup's bass side
compensations.why: Les Paul neck humbuckers are the classic source of woofy, muddy lead tones.

compensations.action: Leads may need less added mid boost and less compression
compensations.why: The guitar already supplies mids and sustain.

general.tip: Set the amp for your dirtiest sound with the guitar volume on 10, then roll back to 6-8 for cleaner rhythm; works best with low/medium-gain, input-sensitive amps and no compressor in front.
general.why: The volume knob lowers the level into the first gain stage, so clipping drops. Vai describes turning the guitar volume down to clear the sound for cleaner songs.

general.tip: Rolling the volume back also dulls the tone unless the guitar has a treble-bleed network (capacitor, or capacitor plus resistor, across the volume pot).
general.why: The pot acts as a voltage divider and highs are lost first; a treble bleed filters bass as you turn down so highs stay prominent. Parallel cap+resistor keeps more highs; a resistor also changes the pot's sweep.

general.tip: Typical treble-bleed starting values: capacitor about 470 pF-1500 pF (0.001 uF is a common start), with a 100k-330k resistor in parallel or about 47k in series if the plain cap is too bright.
general.why: The capacitor sets which frequencies are kept, the resistor sets how bright it gets; sources disagree on exact values.

general.tip: Humbucker height starting point: 3/32 in (2.4 mm) from pole top to string bottom on both E strings, measured with the strings fretted at the last fret; then adjust half a turn either way by ear.
general.why: Seymour Duncan's own general rule; the sweet spot depends on guitar, pickup and string gauge.

general.tip: If a pickup is boomy/woofy on the low strings or shrill on the high strings, lower it (bass side or treble side) a quarter turn at a time before reaching for EQ.
general.why: Too close raises output but hurts clarity and can choke string vibration and sustain; further away is clearer with less output.

general.tip: Balance neck and bridge pickup levels by height so switching pickups does not change how hard the amp is driven.
general.why: A louder neck pickup into a gain preset adds mud and compression exactly where it is least wanted.

general.tip: On the DK24, treat tone at 10 (no-load) as the 'bright switch on' position and 8-9 as normal.
general.why: At 10 the tone circuit is bypassed completely, giving a stronger and more defined signal than a standard pot at full.

general.tip: Dial presets at the level you will actually use them; a preset made quietly will be boomy and harsh loud, and one made loud will seem thin and dull quietly.
general.why: Equal-loudness contours: at low level the ear is less sensitive to lows and highs; a slightly dull, mid-heavy tone at home usually sounds right at stage level (aim near 85 dB for dialing).

general.tip: A close-mic'd cab model has more bass and treble than the same cab heard in a room, and headphones remove all room reflections; add low/high cuts and a little room rather than expecting an amp-in-the-room sound.
general.why: The modeler reproduces the recorded (mic'd) sound by design.

general.tip: On the Quad Cortex cab block, moving the virtual mic away from the cone centre darkens the tone and increasing its distance reduces low end; community starting points are a low cut around 100-125 Hz and a high cut around 5.5-8 kHz for high gain.
general.why: User-forum consensus, not official Neural DSP guidance.

_meta.purpose: Guitar-tone vocabulary, ordered remedies, technique symptoms, recipes and guitar notes for interpreting plain-language tone requests on a modeler (Quad Cortex).
_meta.remedy_order_semantics: Each remedies list is ordered: earlier items are what the community tries first. 'when' holds the condition ('' = always applicable). Changing amp family/channel is filed under amp_gain; low/high cut in the cab block is filed under post_eq because it acts after the amp.
_meta.hz_semantics: hz is the frequency region [low, high] in Hz most associated with the word; null where the word is mainly a dynamic/temporal/spatial property. Ranges are rules of thumb; sources differ by up to an octave.
_meta.basis_semantics: 'cited' = the source page states the specific frequency/mechanism used; 'consensus' = widely repeated community knowledge, with one representative URL.

order_rules.rule: Mud/flub under high gain is fixed BEFORE the distortion
order_rules.common_wrong_first_move: Cutting bass on the amp EQ or with a post EQ
right_order: Tube Screamer-type boost (drive 0, level up) and/or low cut ~100-150 Hz before the amp
order_rules.why: Lows that reach the clipping stages turn into flub and intermodulation that no later EQ can remove.

order_rules.rule: Fizz is not a Treble-knob problem
right_order: move the mic off the dust cap toward the cone edge
high cut (8-10 kHz, lower for high gain)
order_rules.why: Fizz is clipping hash in narrow 4-10 kHz peaks shaped by speaker and mic; Treble mostly sets bite and definition.

order_rules.rule: Thin leads need mids, not more gain or bass
right_order: post-EQ body 200-300 Hz and 700 Hz-1.5 kHz
order_rules.why: Single notes carry little energy; midrange and compression make them sound thick.

order_rules.rule: Too much gain is the usual cause of lost note definition, noise and a small sound
order_rules.common_wrong_first_move: Adding gain to sound heavier or to sustain more
right_order: lower gain until notes just clean up
compressor/delay for sustain instead of gain
order_rules.why: Gain compresses transients and raises noise, fizz and intermodulation; recorded heavy tones use less gain than they seem to.

order_rules.rule: Boxiness appears after scooping the lows
order_rules.common_wrong_first_move: Cutting more bass / raising the low cut further
right_order: move the mic or change the cab/IR
order_rules.why: With lows (and highs) removed, the 300-800 Hz cab resonance is all that is left exposed.

order_rules.rule: Great alone, gone in the band
order_rules.common_wrong_first_move: Turning up, or adding bass and treble
right_order: bass down (leave lows to bass guitar and kick)
order_rules.why: The midrange is the one band where guitar is not competing with bass, kick and cymbals; a scooped tone only sounds huge solo.

order_rules.rule: Quiet monitoring sounds dull and thin; loud monitoring sounds boomy and harsh
order_rules.common_wrong_first_move: EQ'ing bass and treble up at low volume (smile curve)
right_order: set a realistic monitoring level (~85 dB) or level-match
keep separate quiet/loud versions if needed
order_rules.why: Equal-loudness contours: the ear loses lows and highs at low level.

order_rules.rule: Harsh top strings above the 12th fret: change pickup before EQ
order_rules.common_wrong_first_move: High cut or Treble down for the whole preset
order_rules.why: The problem is local to short string lengths on the bridge pickup; global darkening dulls everything else.
A loud cab feeds energy back into the strings; headphones give none, so sustain has to come from compression and ambience.

academic_notes.note: SocialEQ (Cartwright & Pardo, ISMIR 2013): 731 crowd sessions, 324 distinct descriptors. Most-taught words: warm (57 sessions), cold, soft, loud, happy, bright, harsh. Highest-agreement EQ descriptor: 'tinny'; learned near-synonyms: tinny ~ hollow, crisp, light, shrill, bright, cold, raspy; deep ~ throbbing, dark; opposites noted: bright/dark, light/heavy.

Audealize (Seetharaman & Pardo, JAES): 2-D word map built from crowd data for EQ and reverb words (e.g. tinny, warm, boomy, underwater, shrill, muffled); nearby words describe similar effects. The per-word curves were not extracted here; socialeq.org/data is said to hold 40-band encodings.

SAFE project: semantic descriptors collected from inside audio plug-ins; 'warm' and 'bright' are the most used timbral adjectives (per secondary summaries; the paper itself was not read in this session).

Sound On Sound 'What's The Frequency?': electric guitar fullness ~240 Hz, bite ~2.5 kHz, mains hum 50/60 Hz; other instruments: warmth 200-400 Hz, honk 1-3.5 kHz, nasal 1-3 kHz, rasp 6-8 kHz, shrillness 5-7.5 kHz.

Sound On Sound 'Guitar Amp Recording': SM57 rolls off below 200 Hz, dips at 300-500 Hz (where muddiness builds) and has a 2-12 kHz presence peak; MD421 has no low-mid suckout; ribbons are smoother; centre of cone brightest, off-axis/edge warmer.
